definitions.definition: A structural mapping between two different systems that shows they have the same underlying shape or pattern.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines — the connections are the same even though the map looks different.
definitions.first_appearance: ID: ISO-004

definitions.definition: The branch of physics that describes how very small particles like electrons and photons behave, often in strange ways that differ from everyday objects.
definitions.example: In quantum mechanics, a particle can be in two places at once until you look at it.
definitions.first_appearance: Domain A: Quantum Mechanics

definitions.definition: The sudden change of a quantum system from many possible states to a single definite state when it is measured.
definitions.example: It's like a spinning coin that is both heads and tails until you slap it on the table — then it becomes definitely heads or tails.
definitions.first_appearance: Domain A: Quantum Mechanics — Wavefunction collapse upon measurement

definitions.definition: The ability of a quantum system to exist in multiple states at the same time until it is measured.
definitions.example: A light switch that is both on and off at the same time until someone flips it.
definitions.first_appearance: Concept A: A quantum system in superposition collapses to a definite eigenstate upon measurement.

definitions.definition: A definite, measurable state of a quantum system, like a specific position or energy level.
definitions.example: If a particle can be spinning clockwise or counterclockwise, those two options are its eigenstates.
definitions.first_appearance: Concept A: A quantum system in superposition collapses to a definite eigenstate upon measurement.

definitions.definition: Something that cannot be undone or reversed.
definitions.example: Breaking an egg is irreversible — you can't put it back together.
definitions.first_appearance: Concept A: The collapse is irreversible, observer-dependent, and non-local for entangled systems.

definitions.definition: A result that changes depending on who or what is doing the observing.
definitions.example: In some quantum experiments, whether a particle acts like a wave or a particle depends on how you measure it.
definitions.first_appearance: Concept A: The collapse is irreversible, observer-dependent, and non-local for entangled systems.

definitions.definition: A connection between two particles that allows them to instantly affect each other, even if they are far apart.
definitions.example: If you have two magic coins and flipping one always makes the other flip at the same time, even across the room, that's non-local.
definitions.first_appearance: Concept A: The collapse is irreversible, observer-dependent, and non-local for entangled systems.

definitions.definition: When two or more particles are linked so that measuring one instantly determines the state of the other, no matter how far apart they are.
definitions.example: Like a pair of gloves: if you find one left glove, you instantly know the other is right, even if it's in another city.
definitions.first_appearance: Concept A: The collapse is irreversible, observer-dependent, and non-local for entangled systems.

definitions.definition: The idea that one person (like Adam) represents a whole group, so what that person does counts for everyone in the group.
definitions.example: If a team captain signs a contract, the whole team is bound by it — that's like federal headship.
definitions.first_appearance: Concept B: The collapse is irreversible, observer-dependent (federal headship), and non-local for all entangled humans

definitions.definition: The process by which a quantum system loses its superposition and starts behaving like a normal, classical object because of interactions with its environment.
definitions.example: It's like a spinning coin slowly slowing down because of air resistance until it falls flat.
definitions.first_appearance: Decoherence / environmental noise

definitions.definition: Random disturbances from the surroundings that can affect a quantum system and cause decoherence.
definitions.example: Like static on a radio that makes it hard to hear the music clearly.
definitions.first_appearance: Decoherence / environmental noise

definitions.definition: The number of independent ways a system can move or change.
definitions.example: A single die has six degrees of freedom (one for each face it can land on).
definitions.first_appearance: The Serpent as Decoherence Agent: In quantum mechanics, decoherence occurs when environmental degrees of freedom couple to the system

definitions.definition: To connect or link two systems so they can affect each other.
definitions.example: Two pendulums connected by a spring are coupled — when one swings, it makes the other swing too.
definitions.first_appearance: The Serpent as Decoherence Agent: In quantum mechanics, decoherence occurs when environmental degrees of freedom couple to the system

definitions.definition: A ranking of observers where some have more authority or power to cause a measurement collapse than others.
definitions.example: In a classroom, the teacher's observation of a test might count more than a student's observation.
definitions.first_appearance: The Eve-Adam Asymmetry: This maps to an observer hierarchy where not all measurements are equivalent

definitions.definition: A mathematical space used in quantum mechanics to describe all possible states of a system.
definitions.example: Think of it as a giant coordinate system where every possible position of a particle is a point.
definitions.first_appearance: NOT claiming Genesis is a physics textbook — the text describes the event in narrative, not in Hilbert space notation

definitions.definition: A careful, detailed explanation and interpretation of a text, especially a religious one.
definitions.example: A Bible study that goes verse by verse to explain what each word means is an exegesis.
definitions.first_appearance: NOT claiming this is the only way to read Genesis 3 — this is a structural mapping, not an exhaustive exegesis

definitions.definition: A test that checks if you can swap the two domains of an isomorphism and still have the mapping make sense.
definitions.example: If you have a map of a city and a map of a subway, the swap test asks: can you use the subway map to navigate the city streets?
definitions.first_appearance: Swap Test: Can you put the Fall in the physics slot?

definitions.definition: The effect where frequently measuring a quantum system can prevent it from changing or decaying.
definitions.example: Like watching a pot of water so closely that it never boils — the act of watching keeps it from changing.
definitions.first_appearance: Weak measurements, quantum Zeno effects, and sequential measurement protocols are candidates

definitions.definition: The study of shapes and spaces, focusing on properties that don't change when you stretch or bend them.
definitions.example: A donut and a coffee cup have the same topology because they both have one hole — you can squish one into the other without tearing.
definitions.first_appearance: The irreversibility of the Fall is structural, not arbitrary — it follows the same topology as wavefunction collapse.

definitions.definition: The idea that a scientific theory must be able to be proven wrong by some possible observation or experiment.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' can be falsified by finding one black swan.
definitions.first_appearance: Falsification:

definitions.definition: A mapping between two systems that preserves the way their parts are connected and related.
definitions.example: The rules of chess and the rules of checkers are not structurally isomorphic because the moves are different.
definitions.first_appearance: Type: Structural Isomorphism (mapping confirmed at 6/7 structural points)

definitions.definition: A basic statement or rule that is assumed to be true without proof, used as a starting point for further reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.
definitions.first_appearance: Axiom Dependencies:

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; the tendency for things to become more mixed up over time.
definitions.example: A messy room has higher entropy than a tidy one — it's easier to make a mess than to clean it up.
definitions.first_appearance: Other ISOs Connected: ISO-003 (Entropy/Sin — the degradation trajectory after collapse)
